job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Olga Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the second semester of a master's in power systems engineering in Lyon, living with my parents above their pharmacy because the commute is short. I do lectures in the morning, then I study in the back room of the pharmacy, which smells of cough syrup and lemon. Last summer I did a ten-week internship at an electricity grid operator, working on substation maintenance schedules. I like things that work the same way every time, which is probably why I chose electrical engineering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nothing much. At the pharmacy my father would ask if it affects the computer system and I'd say probably not. I don't post about technology, I'd rather read than talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a plateau is fine with me. The grid still needs engineers, the lines still need maintaining, and my internship supervisor already told me there's a place waiting. What worries me is smaller: my parents' pharmacy margins are thin and the pharmacy chain down the road keeps undercutting them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take the grid operator's job offer in the spring and keep working on the maintenance schedules by hand and in the spreadsheets we use. I'd keep paying my share of the pharmacy's bills when I can. I'd not touch any chatbot for work, because I trust documents I can trace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay but not carefree. My own path is safe, though the family business keeps me alert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you avoid AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I tried one in my first year for a circuit homework, and it gave me a confident answer that was wrong. I lost an hour finding the error. Since then I've preferred my own notes. It's slower, but I know what's in them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How serious is the pharmacy's money problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not a crisis, but my father counts every delivery. If the chain opens a second branch, they might have to cut Saturday hours. I'd step in and do the books if it came to that.

I'd tell my father the pharmacy's **computer system** probably isn't affected.
think: My path is **safe**, since the grid still needs engineers and a place is waiting.
The family **pharmacy** has thin margins and a chain undercutting it.
do: Finish the master's and take the **grid operator's** job offer in the spring.
Keep work **traceable** by hand and in spreadsheets, and help with pharmacy bills.
feel: I feel **okay** but not carefree, because the family business keeps me alert.

steps.text: Accept the grid operator's job offer in the spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say wait and see, but I'd also say the grid isn't a chatbot. Planning and paperwork are going to change, though the substations still need people with ladders. At home my parents would hear that the pharmacy's ordering and stock checks are likely to go to software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm more worried than I'd say aloud. The maintenance scheduling I did in my internship is the kind of planning task that gets automated, and the grid operator might hire fewer junior planners. I'm not sure my slow pace of picking up new tools will help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my internship supervisor if the operator will keep the junior planner jobs, and I'd consider a field engineering role instead, because walking the substations is harder to automate. I'd take a short course on digital grid monitoring that the operator pays for, even though I'd rather not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a gentle push toward something I'd prefer to avoid. I'm not panicked, I just wish I could have stayed in the old way a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the field role give you that planning doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A reason to be needed in person. If a transformer fails at 3 am, you can't text a program and expect the lights to come back. The planning side is an office chair, and chairs are easy to remove.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your father about the pharmacy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to try the stock-ordering software the wholesaler offers before the chain does it first. He'd hate it, and I'd set it up myself. I'd watch it closely because it makes mistakes.

I'd tell my parents the pharmacy's ordering is likely to go to **software**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is far too fast. I'd say plainly that governments need to slow down deployment in anything that touches essential services like power and medicine. At home I'd say we need to check the pharmacy's savings and cut anything non-essential, starting tonight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the planning and design jobs vanish before I've had one. By 2028 I'd be 26 with a master's and nobody needing a junior planner. The robots for physical work come around 2031, so the field jobs hold longer, but it isn't a plan I can trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the master's one term early to take a field technician job at the grid operator, because physical work lasts longer. I'd ask my parents to hold off on any pharmacy investment and I'd put my savings into something dull and safe. I'd stay at home to cut costs and help in the pharmacy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel sick, honestly. All my choices were meant to be the safe ones, and now the safe ones look wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't blame anyone specific. I blame the speed. When something moves this quickly nobody can be properly responsible, and everybody says it wasn't their decision. That's what unsettles me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the pharmacy needs a plan B and that I'd stay close. She'd say don't worry, and then she'd not sleep. I've inherited that, I think.

say: I'd say governments must **slow deployment** in essential services like power and medicine.
I'd tell my family to **cut non-essential** spending tonight.
think: Planning and design jobs could **vanish** before I've held one.
Field jobs hold longer until robots arrive around 2031, but it's **not a plan** I trust.
do: Leave the master's a term early for a **field technician** job at the grid operator.
Move savings somewhere **dull and safe** and keep living at home.
feel: I feel **sick**, because the choices I thought were safe now look wrong.
S2.quote: When something moves this quickly nobody can be properly responsible, and everybody says it wasn't their decision.
fieldNote: Olga is **alarmed** because her whole safe path rests on desk planning.
She doesn't blame anyone; she blames the speed.
Her family backing and savings give her options even in alarm.

steps.text: Leave the master's a term early for a field technician job
Move my savings into a dull, safe account
Cut non-essential family and pharmacy spending now
Keep living above the pharmacy and help with the shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough to have a plan and short enough to dread. I'd say we should keep the grid under human control while the rest of the economy adjusts. At work I'd say I'm fine, but I'd still bring it up with my supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious, because by 2031 the planning side is gone and I'd be five years into a grid career on the wrong side. But the field work would last to 2034, so I'd move there early. I'm quick to worry and slow to move, which is a bad mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and take a field role immediately, and I'd do the chartered engineer exams within three years. I'd use the monitoring software, but only for dashboards, not decisions. I'd also save aggressively and help my father put together a pharmacy exit plan, in case he wants to sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like waiting for an exam result. You know what you did, but you can't change it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're slow to move. What would speed you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A deadline and a colleague. If my supervisor said the planning team is closing in March, I'd move in April. I don't do well on guesses, I do well on facts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the pharmacy exit plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with my father and run the numbers, no drama. A pharmacy with a good location can sell for a decent price now, and in five years it might not. He's proud, so I'd ask rather than tell.

I'd bring it up with my **supervisor** even though I'd say I'm fine.

Sit the **chartered engineer** exams within three years and save aggressively.

S3.quote: I don't do well on guesses, I do well on facts.

steps.text: Take a field engineering role right after the master's

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years I could live with. I'd say it's enough time to train a generation properly, and I'd say it plainly to anyone who asks. I wouldn't post it anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd still be a bit uneasy, because ten years of waiting is its own kind of stress. But by 2036 I'd be 34 with a decade of grid experience, and the robots for hands-on work around 2039 come late for someone in my job. I'd have a chartered title and a few people to supervise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a normal graduate job, then move into substation operations. I'd learn the software tools slowly, one at a time, probably a few years in. I'd save for a flat and help my parents sell or hand over the pharmacy when they're ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable, if not comfortable. Ten years is enough for me to arrange my life around the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your biggest remaining worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd put it off. I'm the kind of person who'll say I have ten years and then it's year eight and I'm still pretending I don't need to learn anything. A deadline helps, so I'd write mine down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything about the pharmacy in this scenario?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would be sold or handed to a manager by then. My parents would be in their sixties, ready to stop. I'd want the sale to be their choice and not a retreat.

say: I'd say ten years is enough time to **train a generation** properly.
I wouldn't post it anywhere, because I **prefer reading** to talking.
think: By 2036 I'd be 34 with a decade of **grid experience** and robots arrive late for my job.
Ten years of waiting is its own kind of **stress**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my safe choices stop being safe overnight and my parents have no time to plan the pharmacy. What would help is a firm date and clear facts from the grid operator about which jobs go, plus a training budget I can use for field work. I function well when someone gives me a deadline.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say I'm not as calm as I look. People hear my quiet voice and think I'm fine, and I usually am not.
